items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that two integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if they have the same remainder when divided by [MATH: n.]

Content:
Moreover, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: n] divides [MATH: a-b.]

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn,]

Content:
where [MATH: k\in\mathbb Z.]

Content:
A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations.

Content:
Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

Content:
[MATH: 22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)]

Content:
The addition property allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding [MATH: 2] to both sides gives

Content:
[MATH: 22 + 2|≡10 + 2|(mod12); 24|≡12|(mod12)]

Content:
which is also a true statement since [MATH: 24] and [MATH: 12] both have a remainder of zero when divided by [MATH: 12.]

Content:
Similarly, the subtraction property allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting [MATH: 9] from both sides of our original statement gives

Content:
[MATH: 22 − 9|≡10 − 9|(mod12); 13|≡1|(mod12)]

Content:
which is a true statement since [MATH: 13] and [MATH: 1] both have a remainder of [MATH: 1] when divided by [MATH: 12.]

Content:
In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

Content:
[MATH: a≡b⟺a + c≡b + c(modn); a≡b⟺a − c≡b − c(modn)]

items.title: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: x + 8 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15),] find an equivalent statement where [MATH: x] is isolated.
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: x + 8 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15),] find an equivalent statement where [MATH: x] is isolated.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The addition property of congruences states that

[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

We use the subtraction property to subtract [MATH: 8] from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

[MATH: x + 8|≡11|(mod15); x + 8 − 8|≡11 − 8|(mod15); x|≡3|(mod15)]

The addition property of congruences states that

[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

We use the subtraction property to subtract [MATH: 8] from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

[MATH: x + 8|≡11|(mod15); x + 8 − 8|≡11 − 8|(mod15); x|≡3|(mod15)]

items.readable_text:
Content:
According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,]

Content:
where [MATH: k \in \mathbb{Z}.] Substituting [MATH: b=0,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn]

Content:
This gives rise to the following important fact:

Content:
> Any integer multiple of [MATH: n] is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: n.]

Content:
For example, the numbers [MATH: 10,] [MATH: -25,] and [MATH: 75] are all are all multiples of [MATH: {\color{blue}5},] so they are all congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: {\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 10|= 2 ⋅ 5≡0|(mod5); − 25|= (− 5) ⋅ 5≡0|(mod5); 75|= 15 ⋅ 5≡0|(mod5)]

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following numbers is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 18?]

  1. [MATH: -45]

  2. [MATH: 42]

  3. [MATH: -54]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following numbers is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 18?]

1. [MATH: -45]
2. [MATH: 42]
3. [MATH: -54]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, recall that

[MATH: a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn,]

where [MATH: k\in\mathbb Z.] In other words, when [MATH: a] is divided by [MATH: n,] there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of [MATH: 18] is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 18.]

So, since [MATH: 18\,|\,(-54),] we obtain

[MATH: -54 \equiv (-3) \cdot {\color{blue}18} \equiv (-3)\cdot 0\equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}18}).]

None of the other options are multiples of [MATH: 18.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Content:
Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

Content:
[MATH: x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)]

Content:
By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

Content:
[MATH: x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.]

Content:
When we add [MATH: 0] to both sides of a congruence modulo [MATH: n], we can form an equivalent congruence by writing [MATH: 0] as an integer multiple of [MATH: n.] This works because every integer multiple of [MATH: n] is congruent to [MATH: 0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).]

Content:
In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that [MATH: {\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})] to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x|≡102|(mod5); x + 0|≡102 + 0|(mod5); x|≡102 + 5 ⋅ (− 20)|(mod5); x|≡102 − 100|(mod5); x|≡2|(mod5)]

Content:
We conclude that [MATH: x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)] is equivalent to [MATH: x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).]

Content:
Our answer is correct because [MATH: 102] and [MATH: 2] both have a remainder of [MATH: 2] when divided by [MATH: 5,] and [MATH: 0 \leq 2 < 5.]

Content:
Note: By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of [MATH: r] that satisfies
[MATH: x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo [MATH: n], we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of [MATH: n.] This works because every integer multiple of [MATH: n] is congruent to zero modulo [MATH: n.]

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that [MATH: {\color{blue}6} \cdot (-3) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}6})] to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

[MATH: x + 0|≡23 + 0|(mod6); x|≡23 + 0|(mod6); ≡23 + 6 ⋅ (− 3)|(mod6); ≡23 − 18|(mod6); ≡5|(mod6)]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

items.title: Date Problems

sections.normalized_html:
The opening ceremony of the first modern Olympic Games was held on April 6th, 1896. Given that January 1st, 1896, was a Wednesday, use congruences to determine the day on which the Olympic Games opened.

Hint: The year 1896 was a leap year since it's divisible by [MATH: 4] and is not an end-of-century year.
sections.readable_text:
The opening ceremony of the first modern Olympic Games was held on April 6th, 1896. Given that January 1st, 1896, was a Wednesday, use congruences to determine the day on which the Olympic Games opened.

Hint: The year 1896 was a leap year since it's divisible by [MATH: 4] and is not an end-of-century year.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1896, and April 6th, 1896.

  • There were [MATH: 2] months with [MATH: 31] days (January and March).

  • There were [MATH: 0] months with [MATH: 30] days.

  • There was [MATH: 1] month with [MATH: 29] days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days [MATH: d] between January 1st and April 6th is given by

[MATH: d = \overbrace{31(2) + 30(0) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to April 1st}} + 5.]

Now, note that [MATH: 31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7).]

Therefore, writing the number [MATH: d] modulo [MATH: 7,] we get the following:

[MATH: d|= 2(31) + 0(30) + 1(29) + 5; ≡2(3) + 0(2) + 1(1) + 5|(mod7); ≡6 + 0 + 1 + 5|(mod7); ≡12|(mod7); ≡5|(mod7)]

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date [MATH: 5] days after January 1st, 1896, namely Monday.

Content:
In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

Content:
[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)]

Content:
It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing [MATH: a\equiv b] in terms of divisibility:

Content:
[MATH: a≡b(modn)|⟺a − b = kn; ⟺(a + c) − (b + c) = kn; ⟺(a + c)≡(b + c)(modn)]

Content:
The subtraction property is proved similarly:

Content:
[MATH: a≡b(modn)|⟺a − b = kn; ⟺(a − c) − (b − c) = kn; ⟺(a − c)≡(b − c)(modn)]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that two integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if they have the same remainder when divided by [MATH: n.]

Content:
Moreover, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: n] divides [MATH: a-b.]

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn,]

Content:
where [MATH: k\in\mathbb Z.]

Content:
A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations.

Content:
Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

Content:
[MATH: 22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)]

Content:
The addition property allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding [MATH: 2] to both sides gives

Content:
[MATH: 22 + 2|≡10 + 2|(mod12); 24|≡12|(mod12)]

Content:
which is also a true statement since [MATH: 24] and [MATH: 12] both have a remainder of zero when divided by [MATH: 12.]

Content:
Similarly, the subtraction property allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting [MATH: 9] from both sides of our original statement gives

Content:
[MATH: 22 − 9|≡10 − 9|(mod12); 13|≡1|(mod12)]

Content:
which is a true statement since [MATH: 13] and [MATH: 1] both have a remainder of [MATH: 1] when divided by [MATH: 12.]

Content:
In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

Content:
[MATH: a≡b⟺a + c≡b + c(modn); a≡b⟺a − c≡b − c(modn)]

---

Item 2 — Example: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: x + 8 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15),] find an equivalent statement where [MATH: x] is isolated.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The addition property of congruences states that

[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

[MATH: a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

We use the subtraction property to subtract [MATH: 8] from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

[MATH: x + 8|≡11|(mod15); x + 8 − 8|≡11 − 8|(mod15); x|≡3|(mod15)]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Integers Congruent to Zero

Content:
According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,]

Content:
where [MATH: k \in \mathbb{Z}.] Substituting [MATH: b=0,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn]

Content:
This gives rise to the following important fact:

Content:
> Any integer multiple of [MATH: n] is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: n.]

Content:
For example, the numbers [MATH: 10,] [MATH: -25,] and [MATH: 75] are all are all multiples of [MATH: {\color{blue}5},] so they are all congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: {\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 10|= 2 ⋅ 5≡0|(mod5); − 25|= (− 5) ⋅ 5≡0|(mod5); 75|= 15 ⋅ 5≡0|(mod5)]

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Integers That Are Congruent to Zero Modulo N

Example Prompt:
Which of the following numbers is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 18?]

1. [MATH: -45]
2. [MATH: 42]
3. [MATH: -54]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, recall that

[MATH: a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn,]

where [MATH: k\in\mathbb Z.] In other words, when [MATH: a] is divided by [MATH: n,] there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of [MATH: 18] is congruent to [MATH: 0] modulo [MATH: 18.]

So, since [MATH: 18\,|\,(-54),] we obtain

[MATH: -54 \equiv (-3) \cdot {\color{blue}18} \equiv (-3)\cdot 0\equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}18}).]

None of the other options are multiples of [MATH: 18.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Item 9 — Tutorial: Simplifying Congruences Using Integers Congruent to Zero

Content:
Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

Content:
[MATH: x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)]

Content:
By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

Content:
[MATH: x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.]

Content:
When we add [MATH: 0] to both sides of a congruence modulo [MATH: n], we can form an equivalent congruence by writing [MATH: 0] as an integer multiple of [MATH: n.] This works because every integer multiple of [MATH: n] is congruent to [MATH: 0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).]

Content:
In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that [MATH: {\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})] to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x|≡102|(mod5); x + 0|≡102 + 0|(mod5); x|≡102 + 5 ⋅ (− 20)|(mod5); x|≡102 − 100|(mod5); x|≡2|(mod5)]

Content:
We conclude that [MATH: x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)] is equivalent to [MATH: x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).]

Content:
Our answer is correct because [MATH: 102] and [MATH: 2] both have a remainder of [MATH: 2] when divided by [MATH: 5,] and [MATH: 0 \leq 2 < 5.]

Content:
Note: By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of [MATH: r] that satisfies
[MATH: x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.]

---

Item 10 — Example: Simplifying Congruences

Which of the following is equivalent to [MATH: x \equiv 23\: (\textrm{mod}\,6)?]

2. [MATH: x \equiv 3 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)]
3. [MATH: x \equiv 5 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo [MATH: n], we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of [MATH: n.] This works because every integer multiple of [MATH: n] is congruent to zero modulo [MATH: n.]

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that [MATH: {\color{blue}6} \cdot (-3) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}6})] to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

[MATH: x + 0|≡23 + 0|(mod6); x|≡23 + 0|(mod6); ≡23 + 6 ⋅ (− 3)|(mod6); ≡23 − 18|(mod6); ≡5|(mod6)]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Content:
